name: Team error
statement: Team error names an error attributed to a team rather than to the person who made it, a category drawn from incident classification rather than from any experiment that measures it.
meaning: Kunihide Sasou and James Reason gave the term its current use, and their argument starts as a complaint about method. Error analysis usually looks at the individual who made the error. In large complex systems most people work in teams or groups, so the unit of analysis is wrong. They proposed a definition of team errors and a taxonomy for them, then applied both to events in the nuclear power, aviation and shipping industries. Their conclusion names four conditions that will cause team errors: deficiencies in communication, deficiencies in resource and task management, an excessive authority gradient, and excessive professional courtesy. The point of the relabelling is practical. Handling human errors as team errors, they write, provides an opportunity to reduce human errors. The categories inside the taxonomy are not set out here, because the paper is closed at Elsevier and only its abstract could be read.

origin.note: The paper is 'Team errors: definition and taxonomy', volume 65, issue 1, pages 1 to 9, published in June 1999. Sasou was at the Human Factors Research Center of the Central Research Institute of Electric Power Industry in Tokyo and Reason at the University of Manchester, according to the affiliations held in the Unpaywall record. The abstract also says the paper relates team errors to Performance Shaping Factors.

evidence: The evidence under the label is incident review, and it reads as such. The Joint Commission's 2024 annual review covers 1,575 sentinel events reported by American healthcare organisations during that year. Team failures appear in its lists of contributing factors. Of the 1,472 factors recorded for unintended retention of a foreign object, a lack of shared understanding or mental model across the care team accounts for 14 per cent, and inadequate team communication before, during or after a shared task for 6 per cent. Of the 1,520 factors recorded for wrong surgery, a time-out that was not performed or was incomplete accounts for 10 per cent, and the shared mental model item for another 10 per cent. Of the 7,774 factors recorded for patient falls, the shared mental model item accounts for 7 per cent and inadequate staff-to-staff communication during handoffs for 6 per cent. Reporting to the Joint Commission is voluntary, and the review states that no conclusions should be drawn about the actual relative frequency of events. Direct observation gives a firmer count. Lorelei Lingard and colleagues watched 48 surgical procedures over 90 hours, involving 94 team members, and recorded 421 procedurally relevant communication events. They classed 129 of those as failures, about 30 per cent of exchanges, and 36.4 per cent of the failures had visible effects on system processes, among them delay, tension, resource waste and procedural error. The taxonomy itself has been carried to a fresh corpus once. Renli Lu, Yan Zhou and Mu Zhou applied the Sasou and Reason framework, with Threat and Error Management, to operating errors held in an air traffic control voluntary safety reporting system, and their abstract puts team errors at 31 per cent of the reported air traffic control errors. Their paper is a conference presentation and the underlying count is not in the abstract.

examples.text: A trainee sees the senior reach for the wrong dose and stays quiet. Tracing the error to the trainee's silence or to the senior's hand misses what the category names, which is the gradient between them that made the silence likely.

Two people are each entitled to verify a figure before a payment goes out, and each assumes the other has done it. The error belongs to neither alone. It belongs to a division of the task that left the check unassigned.

examples.tag: Too polite to query the specialist
examples.text: A crew member doubts the course the navigator has set and treats questioning it as rudeness towards a colleague's speciality. Professional courtesy is one of the four conditions named for team errors, and it works by making a correction feel like an insult.

replication.headline: No repeat of Sasou and Reason's coding of industrial events was found, and the measured work sits in the adjacent literature, where the pooled link between teamwork and clinical performance is r = 0.28.
replication.detail: Jan Schmutz, Laurenz Meier and Tanja Manser pooled 31 studies covering 1,390 teams in acute care settings. The sample-size weighted correlation between a teamwork process and clinical performance was r = 0.28, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.35, with Q of 53.7 and I-squared of 46.0 in their Table 3. The split that matters is by what was measured. The 27 samples scored on process performance gave r = 0.30, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.39, and the four scored on outcome performance gave r = 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.23. Their omnibus test of moderators was not significant, F = 0.18 on 6 and 18 degrees of freedom, p > 0.20, across professional composition, team familiarity, team size, task type, patient realism and the type of performance measure. Ashley Hughes and colleagues meta-analysed 129 healthcare team-training studies across 146 independent samples. Training moved learning by a corrected d of 0.89, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.11 over 79 samples, and on-the-job transfer by 0.67, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.82 over 63. Medical errors are one facet of skill-based transfer in their scheme, and the eight samples that measured them, 330 participants in all, gave -0.50, 95% CI -0.88 to -0.13. Their results criterion moved by 0.37 over 47 samples, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.52, and inside it reported safety climate moved by 0.31 over 24 samples while patient mortality moved by -0.36 over five. Angela O'Dea, Paul O'Connor and Ivan Keogh pooled 20 crew resource management evaluations in acute care. Table 5 of their accepted manuscript gives knowledge d = 1.05 over three studies, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.26, attitudes d = 0.28 over nine studies, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.34, and behaviour d = 0.72 over eight studies, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.25. Only two studies could be pooled on clinical care outcomes, both on length of hospital stay, and they gave d = 0.17, 95% CI 0 to 0.33. Amy Starmer and colleagues ran a handoff programme across nine paediatric residency training programmes and reviewed 10,740 admissions, 5,516 before the intervention and 5,224 after. The medical-error rate fell 23 per cent, from 24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions, and preventable adverse events fell 30 per cent, from 4.7 to 3.3 per 100 admissions, both at p < 0.001. Six of the nine sites showed significant error reductions. Non-preventable adverse events did not move, at 3.0 and 2.8 per 100 admissions, p = 0.79. The authors write that their design precludes definitively establishing a causal link between the handoff bundle and improved patient safety.

limits: Sasou and Reason's paper is closed at Elsevier. On 21 September 2026 Unpaywall listed no open location for it, OpenAlex recorded it as closed with no repository copy, and Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC and general web search turned up no readable copy. Its abstract was read three times, in the raw HTML of the colab.ws mirror, in the OSTI ETDEWEB record and in the Elsevier text those two carry, and the three agree word for word. The counts of nuclear, aviation and shipping events the paper analysed are not in that abstract and are left out, as are the categories of the taxonomy itself. The previous version of this page said that an application of the taxonomy to air traffic control sat behind a firewall and was not read. The PDF at the host repository does return a bot challenge, and the abstract and full citation are openly deposited in that repository's OAI feed and on its landing page, where both were read. Lingard and colleagues were previously cited here from a PubMed abstract. The full text is free at PubMed Central and was read there, and the publisher's own PDF returns a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall. Hughes and colleagues are quoted from the author manuscript deposited at PsycNet, read twice; the version of record is listed as open at the publisher and every route to it returns an Incapsula bot challenge, so it was not opened. O'Dea and colleagues are quoted from the accepted manuscript in the University of Galway repository, which is open under a Creative Commons licence. Their published abstract gives attitudes as d = 0.22 and behaviours as d = 1.25. Those two figures are the bounds of the intervals in Table 5 of that manuscript, whose means are 0.28 and 0.72, and the paper's own text calls the attitude effect small. The version of record is paywalled at Oxford Academic, so whether its table matches the manuscript could not be checked. Starmer and colleagues were previously cited here from a PubMed abstract; the typeset article deposited at Washington University was read, the repository serving it through a bot challenge that a mirror of the same file did not. Sydor and colleagues' full text is paywalled at Oxford Academic and the publisher's other host returns 403 to automated requests, so only the abstract was read and the group sizes are unknown. Searches on 21 September 2026 of Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Europe PMC, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, the OSTI ETDEWEB record, the CORE Scholar repository and general web search found no re-coding of the 1999 events by anyone else, and no published test of how reliably two coders assign the same team error category to the same event. OpenAlex answered single-record lookups on the day of this check but returned rate-limit errors on its citation queries, so its list of the 190 works citing the 1999 paper was read through Semantic Scholar instead. The Joint Commission figures are shares of coded contributing factors rather than rates of events, and the underlying reports are voluntary. Schmutz and colleagues' correlation is observational, and only four of their 31 samples scored an outcome rather than a process. Hughes and colleagues' effect on errors rests on eight samples and 330 participants. Starmer and colleagues compared a period before their intervention with a period after it, without a control group.
misreadings: The name suggests a bias, and no laboratory demonstration stands behind it. Team error is a category in an incident taxonomy, and the entries it gets confused with are effects with experiments attached. Groupthink, entry no. 36, is a claim about decision quality flowing from concurrence seeking. Group polarisation, entry no. 267, is a claim about the direction an average moves after discussion. Team error is a claim about who gets counted when an error is traced. The second misreading is redundancy. A second pair of eyes is assumed to catch what the first missed, and Sasou and Reason's own conclusion names an excessive authority gradient and excessive professional courtesy among the causes. Sydor and colleagues randomised 49 anaesthesia trainees in postgraduate years 2 to 5 to a simulated crisis run by a hierarchical or a non-hierarchical theatre team, in which a consultant ordered blood for a Jehovah's Witness. The manipulation moved nothing. Advocacy-inquiry scores did not differ between the groups, p = 0.832, though they rose from year 2 to year 5, p = 0.026. Checking of the blood ran at 92 per cent against 76 per cent, p = 0.082, and administration at 62 per cent against 57 per cent, p = 0.721. This is a simulator study, and it measured what trainees did in a scripted scenario rather than in theatre. The third misreading is treating a contributing-factor table as a table of causes. A factor coded during a root cause analysis records what a reviewing team wrote down afterwards, with the outcome already known. The fourth is reading the training meta-analyses as evidence on patients. Hughes and colleagues move reported safety climate by 0.31 and patient mortality by -0.36 on five samples, and O'Dea and colleagues could pool only two studies on a clinical outcome and found no effect.
